title: Netanyahu Sought Saudi Approval to Join Houthi Strikes; Riyadh Said No
excerpt: Working through US mediators, Israel's prime minister asked to join the campaign against Yemen's Houthis — partly to advance normalisation — but Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman opposed direct Israeli participation, according to Haaretz.
body:
• Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu asked, through US mediators, for Saudi Arabia's approval for Israel to join the military campaign against Yemen's Houthi rebels, according to a diplomatic source cited by Haaretz.
  • Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman opposed direct Israeli participation, fearing a public backlash inside the kingdom, and Anatolia and Israeli media report Riyadh rejected the bid.
  • Netanyahu's outreach had a second goal: using joint action against the Houthis to build toward a Saudi-Israeli normalisation deal, which Riyadh still conditions on progress toward a Palestinian state.
  • For Indians in the Gulf, the stakes are direct: Houthi attacks have already hit Riyadh's airport, where an Indian national died, and the group controls Yemen's side of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, through which roughly 12% of global trade passes.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought Saudi Arabia's approval for Israel to join military operations against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, working through US mediators, but Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman rejected direct Israeli participation, according to a diplomatic source cited by Haaretz and reported by The Business Standard and other outlets. Anadolu reported the same outcome: Saudi Arabia turned down the Israeli bid.

Two goals behind the request

The outreach had two objectives, the sources said. The first was operational: Saudi support for Israeli involvement in counter-Houthi operations along the Red Sea. The second was diplomatic: Netanyahu hoped shared military action would strengthen ties with Riyadh and lay the groundwork for a formal normalisation agreement between Israel and Saudi Arabia.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly promoted Saudi-Israeli normalisation under the Abraham Accords framework. An agreement appeared close in late 2023, before the October 7 Hamas attack and the war in Gaza derailed the effort. Saudi Arabia has since maintained that formal ties require substantial progress toward an independent Palestinian state — a condition Netanyahu, who has pledged to prevent Palestinian statehood, rejects.

Why the Houthi fight has widened

The diplomatic manoeuvring comes amid escalating fighting in Yemen and growing threats to Red Sea trade. In early September, Houthi forces advanced along Yemen's western coast, capturing the port city of Mokha and several Red Sea islands, giving the group control of Yemen's side of the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Saudi-backed forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government later recaptured Mokha amid continued heavy fighting.

The Houthis have also intensified attacks on Saudi targets, including repeated strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The Videshi has covered the fallout from those attacks, including the death of an Indian national and an embassy stay-indoors advisory, as well as the extended closure of Riyadh's airport as Saudi Arabia tracked new drone and missile threats. Saudi officials have told the Wall Street Journal that the kingdom's Patriot interceptor stocks are running short after the airport was hit on consecutive days.

What it means for the region — and for Indians there

A direct Israeli role in the Yemen campaign would mark a sharp escalation and a public alignment Riyadh has so far been unwilling to accept, even as both countries face the same Houthi threat. For the more than eight million Indians who live and work in the Gulf, the practical questions are unchanged: whether Saudi airspace stays open, whether Red Sea shipping — and the trade and remittance flows that depend on it — holds, and whether the conflict pulls in more parties. Netanyahu's rejected bid suggests that, for now, coordination will stay indirect and US-mediated.

What's next

Watch Washington. Trump has said he is evaluating whether the United States should join strikes against the Houthis, and US mediation remains the only channel through which Israeli-Saudi military cooperation is being discussed. Any shift in the Saudi position would likely come tied to the normalisation track — and to movement, however unlikely at present, on the Palestinian statehood condition.
